chapterNote: A chapter of proverbs on folly's disproportionate power, picking up 9:18's closing note — one sinner destroys much good — and running it through court, workshop, and dinner table. Dead flies spoil the perfumer's whole jar; a little folly outweighs a reputation built on wisdom and honor. The fool advertises himself just by walking down the road; the courtier keeps his post and his composure when the ruler's temper rises; and the world's ladders run upside down, folly enthroned on the heights while princes walk like servants. The workman proverbs (vv. 8-11) all teach one lesson: foresight — the pit, the wall-snake, the blunt axe, the serpent charmed too late. Then the tongue: the wise man's words carry grace, while the fool's lips swallow their owner, beginning in foolishness and ending in wicked madness. The chapter closes on the state of a whole land — cursed under boy-kings and breakfast-drunk princes, blessed under noble discipline — with a last word of prudence: do not curse the king even in your thoughts, for a little bird will carry the sound.

1.text: Dead flies make the perfumer's oil stink and ferment, and so does a little folly to a man weighed down with wisdom and honor.
1.amp: Dead [mavet] flies ['flies of death', the KJV margin] cause the ointment [shemen] of the apothecary [raqach — the perfumer, the ointment-blender] to send forth [naba — bubble up] a stinking savour [baash]: so does a little [meat] folly [sikhluth] to him that is in reputation [yaqar — precious, weighty] for wisdom [chokmah] and honour [kabod].
1.notes: The raqach's (H7543) whole jar is worth less than the flies that died in it: corruption is small, cheap, and totalizing. yaqar (H3368) is preciousness by weight — and one meat (H4592), one little folly, moves the scale against years of chokmah and kabod (cf. 9:18).

2.text: A wise man's heart leans to his right hand, but the heart of a fool leans to his left.
2.amp: A wise man's [chakam] heart [leb] is at his right hand [yamin]; but a fool's [kesil] heart at his left [semol].
2.notes: The yamin (H3225), the right hand, was the side of skill, favor, and protection throughout Scripture; the left (H8040, semol) its weaker shadow. The proverb maps orientation, not anatomy: the leb of each man leans toward what it is made of.

3.text: Even walking down the road the fool's understanding fails him, and he announces to everyone he passes that he is a fool.
3.amp: Yea also, when he that is a fool [sakal] walks [halak] by the way [derek], his wisdom ['his heart', leb, the KJV margin] fails [chaser] him, and he says [amar] to every one that he is a fool [sakal].
3.notes: The sakal (H5530) needs no stage; the derek (H1870), the ordinary road, is enough. His empty leb broadcasts itself in gait, mouth, and judgment — the one message he delivers free to every passerby is his own diagnosis.

4.text: If the ruler's temper rises against you, do not abandon your post, for a calm and healing spirit lays great offenses to rest.
4.amp: If the spirit [ruach] of the ruler [mashal] rise up [alah] against you, leave [yanach] not your place [maqom]; for yielding [marpe — healing, a cure] pacifies [yanach — lays to rest] great [gadol] offences [chet].
4.notes: marpe (H4832) is literally healing: composure as medicine applied to a hot room. yanach (H3240) does double duty — do not leave your maqom, and calmness leaves great chet (H2399) at rest. The counsel completes 8:3: neither bolt nor blaze.

5.text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, the kind of error that goes out from the face of the one in power:
5.amp: There is [yesh] an evil [ra] which I have seen [raah] under the sun [shemesh], as an error [shegagah] which proceeds [yatsa] from before [panim — 'from before', the KJV margin] the ruler [shallit]:
5.notes: shegagah (H7684) is the inadvertent error, the slip — but a slip signed at the top, yatsa from the ruler's own panim, becomes policy. The next two verses describe what the slip looks like when it lands.

6.text: Folly is seated on the great heights, while the rich and able sit in the low place.
6.amp: Folly [sekel] is set [natan] in great [rav] dignity ['in great heights', marom, the KJV margin], and the rich [ashir] sit [yashab] in low place [shephel].
6.notes: marom (H4791) is the exalted height, and the folly-word here (H5529, sekel) is planted there by appointment, natan (H5414). The ashir (H6223) stands in for the capable and established: the social ladder inverted by one ruler's error.

7.text: I have seen servants mounted on horses, and princes walking the ground on foot like servants.
7.amp: I have seen [raah] servants [ebed] upon horses [sus], and princes [sar] walking [halak] as servants upon the earth [eretz].
7.notes: The sus (H5483) was rank made visible, the mount of nobility and war. ebed (H5650) riding while the sar (H8269) walks is verse 6 in street clothes: not a moral judgment on servants but a snapshot of order overturned.

8.text: The man who digs a pit may fall into it, and whoever breaks through a wall, a serpent may bite him.
8.amp: He that digs [chaphar] a pit [gummats] shall fall [naphal] into it; and whoso breaks [parats — breaches] an hedge [gader — a wall, a fence], a serpent [nachash] shall bite [nashak] him.
8.notes: Proverbs of recoil: the trap-digger's own naphal (H5307), and the nachash (H5175) nesting in the very gader being breached (parats, H6555). Actions carry their consequences inside them, coiled and waiting (cf. Psalm 7:15).

9.text: Whoever quarries stones may be hurt by them, and the one who splits logs is endangered by them.
9.amp: Whoso removes [nasa — quarries, pulls out] stones [even] shall be hurt [atsab] with them; and he that cleaves [baqa — splits] wood [ets] shall be endangered [sakan] thereby.
9.notes: Even honest work bites: the quarry and the woodpile, not just the trap and the breach. atsab (H6087) is to be hurt or grieved — risk rides along with every even (H68) and every swing at the ets, which is precisely why the next verse commends the sharpened edge.

10.text: If the axe-iron is dull and no one sharpens the edge, then the work demands more and more strength; but wisdom has the advantage of making the stroke succeed.
10.amp: If the iron [barzel] be blunt, and he do not whet [qalal — make light, sharpen] the edge [panim — the face of the blade], then must he put to [gabar] more strength [chayil]: but wisdom [chokmah] is profitable [yithron] to direct [kasher — to make succeed].
10.notes: The blade's edge is its panim (H6440), its face. qalal (H7043), elsewhere 'to curse' as making-light, here means lightening the blade to sharpness; without it the worker spends chayil (H2428), raw strength, on what a whetstone would have spent minutes on. chokmah is yithron (H3504) — the profit-word — because it makes the stroke kasher, succeed.

11.text: If the serpent bites before it is charmed, then the master of the tongue has gained nothing.
11.amp: Surely the serpent [nachash] will bite [nashak] without enchantment [lachash — the charm, the whispered spell]; and a babbler ['the master of the tongue', baal lashon, the KJV margin] is no better [yithron — has no profit].
11.notes: The snake-charmer's craft is worthless a second after the strike: skill unapplied in time is no skill. The baal lashon (H1167, H3956), the master of the tongue, learns the timing lesson of the whole workman-series — yithron (H3504) belongs to those who act before the bite.

12.text: The words of a wise man's mouth are grace itself, but the lips of a fool swallow their own master.
12.amp: The words [dabar] of a wise man's [chakam] mouth [peh] are gracious ['grace', chen, the KJV margin]; but the lips [saphah] of a fool [kesil] will swallow up [bala — engulf, devour] himself.
12.notes: chen (H2580), grace and favor: the chakam's speech blesses the room it enters. bala (H1104) is to swallow whole, the flood-and-Sheol word — the kesil's own saphah (H8193) closes over him like water; his mouth is his undertow.

13.text: The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness, and the end of his talk is wicked madness.
13.amp: The beginning [techillah] of the words [dabar] of his mouth [peh] is foolishness [sikhluth]: and the end [acharit] of his talk ['his mouth', the KJV margin] is mischievous [ra] madness [holelut].
13.notes: The fool's speech has a trajectory: techillah (H8462) in sikhluth (H5531), acharit (H319) in ra holelut — folly compounding into harmful madness by the time he stops. Nothing corrects mid-sentence, because nothing in him is listening.

14.text: And still the fool multiplies words, though no man knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?
14.amp: A fool [sakal] also is full of ['multiplieth', rabah, the KJV margin] words [dabar]: a man [adam] cannot tell [yada] what shall be; and what shall be after [achar] him, who can tell [nagad] him?
14.notes: The sakal talks most confidently about the one subject no one holds: tomorrow. The book's refrain of unknowing (cf. 6:12; 8:7) here becomes satire — rabah (H7235) words about what no nagad (H5046), no telling, can reach.

15.text: The toil of fools wears every one of them out, for he does not even know the way to the city.
15.amp: The labour [amal] of the foolish [kesil] wearies [yaga] every one of them, because he knows [yada] not how to go [yalak] to the city [ir].
15.notes: yaga (H3021), to be worn out: the fool works hard at everything but the one thing that matters — direction. Missing the road to the ir (H5892), the plainest route in the district, he turns amal into pure exhaustion, effort without arrival.

16.text: Woe to you, O land, when your king is a boy and your princes are feasting in the morning!
16.amp: Woe [iy] to you, O land [eretz], when your king [melek] is a child [naar — a boy, a youth], and your princes [sar] eat [akal] in the morning [boqer]!
16.notes: naar (H5288) can mean immature in judgment as much as young in years (cf. Isaiah 3:4). The sarim at table in the boqer (H1242), the hours made for judgment and work, tell the whole story: appetite has replaced government at the top.

17.text: Blessed are you, O land, when your king is nobly born and your princes eat at the proper hour — for strength, and not for drunkenness!
17.amp: Blessed [esher — oh the happiness] art thou, O land [eretz], when your king [melek] is the son [ben] of nobles, and your princes [sar] eat [akal] in due season [et], for strength [geburah], and not for drunkenness [shethi]!
17.notes: esher (H835) is the 'blessedness' exclamation of Psalm 1:1, pronounced over a whole eretz. The same table, the same food — the difference is the et (H6256), the fitting time, and the purpose: geburah (H1369), strength for service, versus the morning cup.

18.text: Through sheer slothfulness the beams sink down, and through idle hands the house drips with leaks.
18.amp: By much slothfulness [atslut] the building [meqareh — the beam-work, the rafters] decays [makak — sinks low]; and through idleness [shiphlut] of the hands [yad] the house [bayith] drops through [dalaph — drips, leaks].
18.notes: atslut (H6103) is the sluggard-word of Proverbs, and makak (H4355), to sink low: roofs fail by neglect, not by attack. dalaph (H1811), the dripping — applied to the bayith it reads as the lazy kingdom of verse 16 in miniature; applied at home it needs no interpreting at all.

19.text: Bread is prepared for laughter, and wine gladdens the living, and money answers for everything.
19.amp: A feast [lechem — bread] is made [asah] for laughter [sechok], and wine [yayin] makes glad the life ['maketh glad the life', samach, chay, the KJV margin]: but money [keseph] answers [anah] all things.
19.notes: In the mouth of the morning-feasters this is a creed — keseph (H3701) as the anah (H6030), the answer, to everything; in the Preacher's mouth it is dry observation of how such courts run. Bread, wine, and money are good servants (cf. 9:7) and absurd masters.

20.text: Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, and do not curse the rich even in your own bedroom, for a bird of the air will carry the sound, and the owner of wings will report what you said.
20.amp: Curse [qalal — make light of, revile] not the king [melek], no not in your thought [madda — your knowing, your conscience]; and curse not the rich [ashir] in your bedchamber [cheder — the innermost room]: for a bird of the air [shamayim] shall carry [yalak] the voice [qol], and that which has [baal] wings [kanaph] shall tell [nagad] the matter [dabar].
20.notes: madda (H4093) reaches into the thought-life itself, and the cheder (H2315) is the innermost room — no venue is sealed. The proverb behind 'a little bird told me': the baal kanaph (H1167, H3671), the owner of wings. Prudence toward power, yes — but also the book's quiet awareness that nothing spoken anywhere is truly unheard (cf. 12:14).
